title: How I Finally Fixed My Sleep Schedule
script: Narrator: [tired] For years, I told myself I simply wasn't a morning person, as though my sleep habits were something fixed rather than something I had shaped myself.
Narrator: [honest] In reality, I stayed up scrolling through my phone until nearly two most nights, then dragged myself out of bed exhausted by seven.
Narrator: [reflective] Even though I felt tired constantly, I convinced myself that coffee could substitute for the sleep I kept refusing to prioritize.
Narrator: [worried] It was only after fainting briefly at work that I finally admitted the problem wasn't my schedule; it was me avoiding rest.
Narrator: [thoughtful] My doctor suggested I try something called sleep hygiene, which sounded oddly clinical for something as simple as going to bed on time.
Narrator: [determined] So I set a firm rule: no screens after ten thirty, even if I wasn't remotely tired yet at that hour.
Narrator: [honest] The first few nights were miserable. I stared at the ceiling, restless, wondering what I was even supposed to do with my hands.
Narrator: [thoughtful] Instead of scrolling, I started reading a physical book, something I hadn't done regularly since university, if I'm being completely honest.
Narrator: [surprised] Within a week, I noticed I was falling asleep faster, despite my initial certainty that nothing would change so quickly.
Narrator: [hopeful] I also began waking up at the same time every day, even on weekends, which my friends thought sounded unnecessarily strict.
Narrator: [warmly] However, that consistency turned out to matter more than anything else, since my body gradually stopped fighting against an unpredictable rhythm.
Narrator: [grateful] My sister, who had struggled with insomnia herself, checked in weekly, which kept me accountable during the weeks I wanted to quit.
Narrator: [proud] By the second month, I no longer needed three cups of coffee just to function through the afternoon.
Narrator: [reflective] I used to see sleep as something I could negotiate with, squeezed in around everything else that felt more urgent.
Narrator: [peacefully] Now I understand that unless I protect my sleep deliberately, everything else in my life quietly suffers because of it.
Narrator: [warmly] If someone had told me a year ago that reading before bed would change so much, I honestly wouldn't have believed them.

quiz.question: What did the narrator originally believe about her sleep habits?
options: That they were fixed and unchangeable, since she wasn't a morning person
That she needed less sleep than most people
That coffee was unnecessary for her
quiz.explanation: She believed her sleep habits were something fixed, telling herself she simply wasn't a morning person.

quiz.question: What event made her finally admit there was a problem?
options: Her doctor forced her to change
quiz.explanation: It was only after fainting briefly at work that she admitted the real problem was avoiding rest.

quiz.question: What rule did she set for herself?
quiz.explanation: She set a firm rule of no screens after ten thirty, even if she wasn't tired yet.

quiz.question: What did she start doing instead of scrolling her phone?
quiz.explanation: She started reading a physical book instead of scrolling, something she hadn't done since university.

quiz.question: What did the narrator learn about waking up at the same time daily?
options: That consistency mattered more than anything else for her sleep
It made her more tired overall
quiz.explanation: She learned that consistency turned out to matter more than anything else, since her body stopped fighting an unpredictable rhythm.
